intro:
These exercises take the order-platform domain model from the chapter and make you handle each part with your own hands: classifying the building blocks, tracing the Draft/Submitted state machine, writing validating newtype constructors, defining the repository seam as a trait, pulling a leaked invariant back onto the aggregate, and designing a persistence boundary for an event-sourced aggregate. The throughline is the chapter's central claim: in Rust the domain model is not enforced by a framework, a base class, or a convention, but by types that refuse to hold an invalid value.

Work them in order. The early exercises pin down the vocabulary and the mechanics of value objects and aggregates; the later ones move outward to the repository trait, the difference between an anaemic and a rich model, and the ownership consequences of doing IO that may suspend. The lab is the small, self-contained version of the whole chapter: an Order aggregate whose invariants live on the model and whose value object rejects zero quantity at construction.

exerciseSolutions.title: Place each building block inside the aggregate boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Sort the listed types into the three DDD roles the chapter uses. Quantity, MoneyCents, and Sku are value objects: each is defined entirely by its value, carries no identity, and rejects invalid local state in its constructor. Quantity::new refuses zero, Sku::new refuses an empty or whitespace-only code, and MoneyCents wraps a u64 amount. Two Quantity(2) values are interchangeable because nothing distinguishes them but the number they hold, which is exactly what makes them value objects rather than entities.

OrderId and CustomerId are identifiers. They are newtypes over a u64 whose whole job is to name a specific entity unambiguously and to keep one kind of id from being passed where another is expected. OrderId in particular derives Eq and Hash so it can serve as a repository key.

Order is the aggregate root. It is the entity that guards the consistency boundary: it owns its OrderLine values and the value objects they carry (Sku, Quantity, MoneyCents), and it owns the Draft/Submitted status that the submit transition advances. The consistency boundary it guards is the whole order — you cannot add a line to a submitted order, and you cannot submit an empty one, because those rules live on Order's methods and the lines and status fields are private to the aggregate.

The repository seam is the single door to persistence. The chapter's rule is that the repository loads and saves the whole aggregate through its root, keyed by OrderId — never an individual OrderLine. There is no repository for lines, because lines have no independent lifecycle; they exist only inside an order.

Order is an entity rather than a value object precisely because it has an OrderId. Two orders with identical lines and identical status are still different orders if their ids differ — identity, not value, decides equality. A value object has the opposite property: strip its identity away and there is nothing left but the value, so equality is value equality.
criteria: Quantity, MoneyCents, and Sku are named as value objects, OrderId/CustomerId as identifiers, and Order as the aggregate root.
The answer states the root owns the value objects and the order lines inside its boundary.
The answer states the repository loads and saves the whole aggregate through the root, keyed by OrderId, not individual lines.
The entity-versus-value-object distinction is stated: Order has identity via OrderId; value objects are defined only by their value.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the order state machine through submit and add_line
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Trace the sequence against the ddd_order_aggregate listing. Start with Order::new, which sets status to Draft and lines to an empty Vec. Two add_line calls follow. Both succeed because the order is still Draft: add_line only rejects when status is Submitted, so each call pushes an OrderLine and returns Ok(()). The lines are now (BOOK-1, qty 2, 1500) and (PEN-9, qty 3, 400).

Next, submit. Because lines is non-empty, the empty-order guard does not fire; submit sets status to Submitted and returns Ok(()). If submit had been called on an order with no lines, it would return Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder) — that is the first thing the method checks.

The second add_line, called after submission, hits the guard at the top of the method: status == Submitted, so it returns Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder) and the line is never pushed. The order is now locked against further modification.

total_cents folds qty.get() as u64 times unit_price.get() over every line: line one contributes 2 * 1500 = 3000, line two contributes 3 * 400 = 1200, summing to 4200. The cast to u64 happens before the multiply so the arithmetic stays in u64.

The reason add_line only ever receives valid values is that Quantity::new and Sku::new run their checks at construction, before a line exists. A zero quantity or an empty Sku is rejected up front and never reaches the aggregate, so add_line does not need to re-validate them. The value-object constructors handle the local rules; the aggregate handles the aggregate-wide rule (you cannot modify a submitted order). Each layer enforces exactly the invariant it owns.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Predicted Results and total for the traced sequence.
criteria: submit on an empty order is identified as Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder).
add_line after submission is identified as Err(DomainError::CannotModifySubmittedOrder).
total_cents is computed as 4200 (2*1500 + 3*400).
The answer notes value-object constructors reject local errors first, so add_line only ever receives valid Quantity and Sku values.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a Sku newtype with a validating constructor
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Sku is a newtype over an owned String whose constructor is the only way to build a valid value. fn new takes &str rather than String so the caller does not have to allocate before the value is known to be valid, and it returns Result<Sku, DomainError> so an invalid code surfaces as a domain error rather than a silently constructed bad value.

The check is value.trim().is_empty(). trim() handles both the empty string and the whitespace-only string in one test, so "" and "   " both fail with Err(DomainError::EmptySku). Only after that check passes does the constructor allocate with value.to_string() and wrap it in Sku. Allocating after validation, not before, means an invalid code never causes an allocation and never produces a Sku value at all.

The accessor as_str returns &str by handing back &self.0. Its lifetime is tied to &self, so the borrow is valid exactly as long as the caller holds the Sku, and no clone is made — reading a Sku is free.

The swapped-parameter bug the newtype prevents is passing the wrong string into a function that expects a product code. If both a customer code and a product code were raw String, the type checker could not tell them apart, and a call site that swapped them would compile and fail at runtime. With distinct newtypes, a customer-code String simply will not type-check where a Sku is required; the mistake becomes a compile error instead of a production bug.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Validating newtype: reject empty/whitespace, allocate after, borrow on read.
criteria: Sku::new returns Err(DomainError::EmptySku) for "" and "   " and Ok for "BOOK-1".
The successful path constructs Sku(value.to_string()) only after the trim check passes.
as_str returns &str borrowed from self.0 rather than a cloned String.
The explanation names that distinct newtypes stop a raw String customer code from being passed where a Sku is expected.

exerciseSolutions.title: Define a Repository trait and an in-memory implementation
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The repository is expressed as a trait so the domain depends on an interface, not on a concrete store. The trait declares two methods. save(&mut self, order: Order) takes the aggregate by value because saving hands the whole order to the store; the store now owns it. find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order> returns a borrowed Option so a read does not clone the aggregate — the caller gets a reference into the store that lasts as long as the borrow of &self.

The in-memory implementation wraps a HashMap<OrderId, Order>. save inserts keyed by order.id; find delegates to self.map.get(&id). For OrderId to be a HashMap key it must derive Eq and Hash (it does in the chapter, deriving PartialEq, Eq, and Hash on the newtype), so two OrderId values hash and compare by their inner u64.

The payoff of depending on the trait rather than on the concrete HashMap is substitutability. The aggregate and the application services name only OrderRepository, never InMemoryOrderRepository or any database type. Swapping the in-memory store for a SQL-backed or remote implementation changes only which concrete type is constructed at the edge of the program; not a line of aggregate logic moves. The trait is the seam that keeps persistence outside the core language of the model.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Repository as a trait seam backed by a HashMap; reads borrow, saves own.
criteria: The trait declares save(&mut self, order: Order) and find(&self, id: OrderId) -> Option<&Order>.
The implementation inserts by order.id and returns self.map.get(&id) from find.
OrderId derives Eq and Hash so it can be a HashMap key.
The answer states that depending on the trait lets infrastructure be swapped without touching aggregate logic.

exerciseSolutions.title: Move a leaked invariant back onto the aggregate
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is an anaemic model. The Order has public lines and status fields and no behavior of its own; the empty-order rule lives in an application handler that checks order.lines.is_empty() before flipping order.status to Submitted by hand. The rule is correct where it is written, but it is in the wrong place. The bug appears the moment a second caller submits an order without copying that check: nothing stops it from setting status = Submitted on an empty order, because the invariant is a convention in one handler rather than a property of the type. An anaemic model invites every caller to re-implement the rule, and re-implementing it means eventually forgetting it.

The fix moves the invariant onto the aggregate. Order::submit performs the is_empty check itself and returns Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder) when the order has no lines, otherwise advancing status to Submitted. The lines and status fields are made private so no caller can mutate them directly; the only way to add a line or change state is through the aggregate's methods. This is how Rust puts behavior near state without inheritance — private fields plus an impl block, no base class required.

With the rule on the model, the handler shrinks to order.submit()? and an error path. It contains no domain rule, only orchestration: call the aggregate method and propagate whatever error it returns. The invariant is now enforced once, at the type, for every caller — there is no version of it left to forget.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Invariant relocated from handler to Order::submit; fields made private.
criteria: The empty-order check is relocated from the handler into Order::submit.
lines and status are private and changed only through aggregate methods.
The refactored handler contains no business rule, only submit() and error propagation.
The answer explains that an anaemic model lets every caller re-implement and forget the invariant.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose between sync and async repositories for an event-sourced aggregate
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The Account aggregate holds no stored balance; its state is the fold of its event stream. The repository therefore deals in events, not in a materialized aggregate, and the store is remote and accessed asynchronously, which is the case the chapter's production rule was written for: if the repository method performs IO and may suspend, return owned data or an owned projection.

Load should return an owned Vec<AccountEvent>, not a borrowed slice. A borrow would have to be tied to something inside the store, but an async load awaits a network round trip — the future may suspend, the connection or buffer it read from may be released across the await point, and there is nothing stable for a &[AccountEvent] to borrow from that outlives the call. Returning owned events sidesteps the lifetime fight entirely: the caller holds the data outright and the store is free to do whatever it needs after the await.

The async signatures take &self and return a Result over owned data. load_events returns Result<Vec<AccountEvent>, RepoError>; append_events takes the new events by value and returns Result<(), RepoError>. Neither return type borrows from the store. Because the methods are async, calling them yields a future the caller awaits; the &self receiver is fine because the borrow lasts only for the duration of the await within the caller, and the returned Vec is owned and outlives it.

Rehydrate consumes the loaded events to rebuild current state. It starts from a fresh, empty accumulator and applies each event in order, exactly as Account::rehydrate does: every apply validates against the state built so far (a deposit before Opened is rejected, a withdrawal beyond the running balance is rejected), mutates the accumulator, and bumps version. Version follows the applied stream length — after folding N valid events, version is N — so it doubles as an optimistic-concurrency token: append_events can refuse to write if the store's current version no longer matches the version the aggregate was rehydrated at.

The accepted cost is the one event sourcing always charges. You gain a complete temporal history of domain facts, but you take on projection and migration work: read models must be rebuilt by replaying the stream when a projection changes, and an evolving event schema forces you to keep deserializing and upcasting old event shapes forever, since past events are immutable facts you cannot retroactively edit.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Async event store returns owned Vec; rehydrate folds the stream and sets version.
criteria: The design returns owned data (Vec<AccountEvent>) from the async load, citing that IO may suspend.
The async signatures take &self and return a Result over owned data, not a borrow tied to the store.
The answer states rehydrate applies each event in order and that version follows the applied stream length.
At least one accepted cost is named: projection rebuilds and/or event-schema migration.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
lines = 2
total cents = 4200
state = submitted
submit ok = true
locked after submit = true
zero qty rejected = true
labSolution.explanation:
The two TODOs sit on the aggregate where the invariants belong. Order::submit checks self.lines.is_empty() first: an empty order returns Err(DomainError::EmptyOrder); otherwise it advances status to Submitted and returns Ok(()). Order::total_cents folds over the lines, multiplying each quantity by its unit price — q.get() as u64 * price — and sums the results. The cast to u64 happens before the multiply so the arithmetic never overflows a u32.

Main builds a Draft order and adds two lines while it is still Draft, so both add_line calls succeed and lines.len() is 2. submit runs against a non-empty order, so it returns Ok and submitted is true; state then reports "submitted". The third add_line runs after submission, hits the status == Submitted guard, and returns Err, so blocked is true and no third line is pushed. Quantity::new(0) fails its own zero check at construction, so zero_qty is true.

The total is 2*1500 + 3*400 = 3000 + 1200 = 4200. Putting these together reproduces the expected output line for line: the value object enforces the zero-quantity rule at construction, and the aggregate enforces the empty-order and no-modify-after-submit rules in its methods — each invariant owned by exactly the type responsible for it.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does Rust enforce a domain model through types that refuse invalid values rather than through a base class or runtime framework?
reviewAnswers.answer: Rust has no inheritance hierarchy to hang shared domain behavior on and no runtime framework that validates objects as they are constructed, so the type system itself is where invariants live. A value object whose only constructor returns Result cannot exist in an invalid state, because the only way to obtain one is to pass the validation. This moves enforcement from runtime — where a framework or convention can be bypassed or forgotten — to compile and construction time, where an invalid value simply cannot be produced. The guarantee is structural, not procedural: there is no code path that yields a bad value to forget to guard.

reviewAnswers.question: When should an invalid state be encoded in a value-object type versus checked in an aggregate method?
reviewAnswers.answer: Encode it in the value-object type when the rule is local and stable — it depends only on the single value being constructed, such as a quantity that must be non-zero or a Sku that must be non-empty. Check it in an aggregate method when the rule depends on aggregate-wide state — such as refusing to submit an empty order or refusing to modify a submitted one, which require knowing the order's lines and status. The chapter's rule is exactly this split: local and stable goes in the type, aggregate-wide goes in the method. Rust gives you both tools, and using the right one keeps each invariant owned by the type that has the information to enforce it.

reviewAnswers.question: What does primitive obsession cost a domain, and how do newtypes such as OrderId and Sku address it?
reviewAnswers.answer: Primitive obsession is modeling domain concepts as raw primitives — every id a u64, every code a String — which erases the distinctions the domain cares about. The cost is swapped-parameter bugs that compile and fail at runtime, validation that has to be repeated at every call site, and logs and signatures that carry no domain meaning. Newtypes like OrderId and Sku wrap the primitive in a distinct type whose constructor validates once, so a CustomerId can no longer be passed where an OrderId is expected and an empty Sku can never be constructed. The small ceremony buys fewer swapped arguments, narrower traits, clearer logs, and a sharp boundary between internal and external identifiers.

reviewAnswers.question: What does it mean to say a rich model in Rust puts behavior near state and invariants without inheritance?
reviewAnswers.answer: A rich model keeps the rules that govern data on the type that owns the data, rather than scattering them across handlers or a service layer. In Rust this means an impl block with methods alongside private fields: the aggregate's methods are the only way to change its state, so the invariants cannot be bypassed. There is no base class with protected fields and no inherited template method — Rust uses impl blocks, value objects, traits, and modules, each doing its own job. The result is the opposite of an anaemic model, where public fields let every caller re-implement and eventually forget the rules.

reviewAnswers.question: In an event-sourced aggregate, how is current state derived from the event stream, and what does the version count track?
reviewAnswers.answer: There is no stored current state to read; the aggregate is rehydrated by folding its event stream into a fresh accumulator one event at a time. Each apply validates the event against the state built so far — a deposit before the account is open is rejected, a withdrawal beyond the running balance is rejected — and mutates the accumulator only when the event is valid. The version count tracks how many events have been applied, so after folding N valid events the version is N, mirroring the applied stream length. That count doubles as an optimistic-concurrency token: an append can be refused when the store's version no longer matches the version the aggregate was rehydrated at.
